label: Faster Grobner Bases
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 547 through 600 and confronts the practical cost of Buchberger's algorithm. Most S-polynomials reduce to zero and waste effort, so refined criteria, better selection strategies, and order conversion make Grobner basis computation feasible on substantial problems.

label: Buchberger's Criteria
notes: Two criteria of Buchberger let us skip many S-polynomial reductions in advance. Pairs whose leading terms are relatively prime reduce to zero automatically, and a chain criterion discards pairs already covered by others, dramatically pruning the work without affecting correctness.

label: Selection Strategies
notes: The order in which S-pairs are processed greatly affects performance. The normal selection strategy, choosing pairs of least leading common multiple, and the sugar strategy, tracking a degree surrogate, keep intermediate polynomials small and speed termination in practice.

label: The FGLM Algorithm
notes: For a zero-dimensional ideal the FGLM algorithm converts a Grobner basis from one monomial order to another using linear algebra in the finite-dimensional quotient ring. This makes it cheap to obtain an elimination-friendly lexicographic basis from a fast graded one.

label: Improved Computation
notes: Modern systems combine these criteria with signature-based methods and modular arithmetic to control coefficient growth, the dominant cost over the rationals. Computing modulo primes and reconstructing answers keeps intermediate numbers small while preserving the exact result.

label: Complexity and Practice
notes: Grobner basis computation has high worst-case complexity, doubly exponential in the number of variables, yet performs well on the structured systems arising in applications. Understanding these limits guides realistic expectations. This closes the main text. Next: the appendices on algebra, pseudocode, and software.
